newsitem.title: USA: IMF willing to support Mexico structural reforms.
newsitem.headline: IMF willing to support Mexico structural reforms.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund is ready to start working with Mexico on a three-year program, IMF managing director Michel Camdessus said Thursday.

"We will start to prepare a three-year program to continue with what has been done over the past 15 months, with quite a degreee of success, as you all know, to splice a far-reaching, structural reforms program with the emergency program," he said at the closing news conference of the IMF/World Bank annual meeting.

The IMF last year granted Mexico an unprecedented $17.8 billion loan as part of an international package that rescued Mexico from a financial collapse caused by the disastrous December, 1994 devaluation of the peso.
In answer to a question about how much money Mexico could eventually secure from the IMF, Camdessus said that would only be discussed once Mexican authorities finish drafting their reform blueprints.
"In a country like Mexico, which is recovering quite rapidly, it's not a problem of financial resources, and if it were, it would only be a very secondary problem," he argued.
Mexico's Finance Secretary, Guillermo Ortiz, said Wednesday his country would try to obtain a "precautionary" loan from the IMF by the first quarter of 1997.
Mexico would only draw on those resources if international capital market conditions worsened and make it difficult for the government to borrow for longer terms and at lower rates.
Ortiz explained that Mexico would need such a cushion for a "hump" in its debt repayment schedule in 1998 and 1999.

In answer to a question from a Mexican reporter who said Ortiz had bristled at the suggestion that the IMF would decide Mexico's economic plan, Camdessus replied: "The Secretary is right to be angry. We never pretend to substitute countries in designing their policies."
